description: This post-event analysis is the report of the Independent Panel Reviewing the Impact of Hurricane Katrina on Communications Networks, which FCC Chairman Kevin Martin established in January 2006 and which submitted its report on 12 June 2006. The panel reviewed the impact of the hurricane of August 2005 on communications infrastructure in Alabama, Louisiana and Mississippi and the public and private response. Katrina knocked out more than three million customer phone lines; dozens of central offices and many miles of outside plant were damaged or destroyed by wind and flooding, more than a thousand cell sites went out of service, more than 35 public safety answering points failed at the height of the storm, and some Louisiana parishes lacked 911 service for weeks. Its recommendations fall into four areas: pre-positioning industry and government for disasters to achieve network reliability and resiliency; improving recovery coordination; improving the operability and interoperability of public safety and 911 communications; and improving communication of emergency information to the public. The FCC opened a rulemaking on them in 2006 and adopted an order in 2007 (FCC 07-107), including backup power requirements. Coverage: the US Gulf Coast, 2005. Format and access: free report and orders on the FCC website and Federal Register notices, US government works. Caveats: impact figures are aggregate and from industry; www.fcc.gov blocks automated readers. Simulation uses: hazard exposure and cascading failure of telecommunications under hurricane and flood, dependence of emergency services on networks, and resilience and emergency response planning. Related records: the FCC 2017 hurricane season report shows later practice.
